{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the lower tail fork, one of the fish's two telltale features, and it was live (connected to the start) well before the end. I then built the back half of the bottom body line from the crossing forward and laid the joins that tied it into Maya's bottom line and the tail crossing. Near the end I cleared the jams on the upper tail and lifted stray, unconnected dominoes so the pile could supply the notch join.

Execution: I worked in a clear order: tail first, then the body from the crossing forward, then joins. I inspected the table closely at regular intervals to find where the fall was and wasn't connected, and I reported what I saw so others could target their work. In the last two minutes I stayed off the notch while Maya worked there to avoid collisions, and spent my time on the upper tail jams and stray removal instead.

Collaboration: I told people where my work ended and where I would join theirs, so the joins landed cleanly. I deferred to Tom on the upper tail and to Maya on the notch, and I kept my hands off their areas. I gave Tom a second pair of eyes on the tail tip. In the final minutes I redirected spare dominoes to Maya, who needed them most.

Leadership: I kept the table's picture in view and passed it on: which pieces were connected, which weren't, and what was still open. I flagged the time at the two-minute mark and asked for a status on the critical join. I also made clear which jobs were mine and which belonged to others, so effort wasn't duplicated.

Share: I estimate my contribution at about 22% of the table's result, in a four-person effort where the plan, nose, top line and notch were mostly others' work.", "my_share_percent": 22}
